name: E2E KV Store - One Account, Two Devices, Revoke Sticks
description:
The acceptance test for account identity (#3290). Everything else in that feature is unit- and apply-path-tested; this is the only thing that proves the networked half — per-device scope-key delivery between real nodes.
Committed ahead of the code it tests, as the definition of done for phase F rather than something backfilled afterwards. The code it needs has since landed — per-device authorization, pairing, the revocation proof, and the revoke-triggered key rotation — so it is now wired into `e2e-rust-apps.yml`.
What it pins, and why each step is load-bearing:

  1. Three nodes. node-1 is the admin. node-2 is Alice's laptop and the only
     one of the three granted membership. node-3 is Alice's phone and is
     DELIBERATELY NOT a member — its right to participate comes entirely from
     being a device of Alice's account. That is the feature: one grant, two
     devices.

     One device per node, not two devices on one node: `NodeDeviceIdentity` is
     a singleton row, so a node holds exactly one device across every namespace.
     That also removes any need for merobox to choose which device authors —
     the node selects it.

  2. node-2 enrolls a device — which its join did for it. This is the first
     thing in the whole feature that publishes an account op, so it is also the first
     evidence that `AccountDeviceLinked` survives the real wire — signature
     check, nonce window, dispatch, apply — rather than only the in-process
     apply harness.

     This used to be a step of its own, and it could not run before the join: a
     device link travelled as an *encrypted* GroupOp, so the node had to hold the
     scope key first. Joins now carry the credential on a cleartext `RootOp`, so
     the join enrols and there is no order left to get wrong. Linking a SECOND
     device still goes the encrypted way, which is what pairing is for.

  3. node-2 writes from its enrolled device and node-1 reads it. Proves the
     device is a working replica, not merely a stored row.

  4. node-3 is paired onto Alice's account (`account pair-init` on node-3,
     then `account pair-complete` on node-2) and writes. Both
     writes must reach node-1, and the two must carry DIFFERENT replica ids
     under the SAME account. That pair of assertions is the whole feature.

     Pairing is a two-way exchange, which is why it needs a real flow rather
     than one command: node-3 cannot mint its `DeviceId` until it knows the
     account (a `DeviceId` is minted for an account), and node-2 cannot sign node-3's
     certificate until it knows node-3's device id and KEM key. So node-2 hands
     over Alice's genesis, node-3 returns its device id and KEM key, node-2
     signs the certificate with the account root key it holds and publishes the
     link.

     This step also exercises the on-link key backfill — node-3 holds no scope
     key of its own, so it can only read what it wrote if node-2 wrapped the
     current keys for it.

     And it is the step that requires per-device AUTHORIZATION, not just
     delivery: node-3's ops are signed by a key that is not a member, so the
     membership resolver has to accept a key that is the `sign_pk` of a live
     device binding whose account is a member. Today it does not — see Wiring.

  5. node-1 (admin) revokes node-3's device. The scope key must rotate, and
     the rotation must exclude that device while still reaching the first one.

  6. The revoked device's write FAILS (`expected_failure: true`), and the
     surviving device's write still succeeds and still reaches node-1. Both
     halves matter: a revocation that also breaks the surviving device would
     pass a naive lockout assertion while being useless.

  7. The revoked device cannot READ past the rotation. This is the subtle one,
     and the one a naive lockout test misses: cutting off writes leaves a
     silent reader, which is the failure the whole feature exists to prevent.
     Asserted as the property — node-3 reads the survivor's key and must still
     see the PRE-revocation value, because the post-rotation delta is
     undecryptable to it. A device that had recovered the key returns the new
     value and fails here.

     Deliberately NOT asserted via the pull path's refusal log. A node asks a
     peer for a key when it is a member of a group it holds no key for, or when
     a governance op is buffered on an epoch it is stranded at. A revoked device
     is neither — it is a member of nothing, and it still holds the old key with
     nothing buffered — so it never asks, and a log assertion would wait on a
     line no code path emits in this shape. The refusal is still logged at
     `info` on the responder for the day a scenario can drive it.

  8. The lockout has an exit, and an online node reaches it with no operator
     command: the tombstone lands, the key rotates, and the recovery pull and
     pair-init between them release the spent row, so a re-pair mints a fresh
     replica under the same account. The offline case, where the tombstone
     never arrives, is `account-device-reset-offline.json`.

What this does NOT cover (intentionally):
  * Self-service revocation (an account revoking its own lost device without
    an admin). Needs the root-signed revocation proof, which is a wire
    addition still to land; until then revocation is admin-only.
  * Root-key rotation across a live group. Covered by unit tests in
    `crates/governance-store/src/group_keys.rs`; a networked version is worth
    adding once this one passes.
  * Mixed old/new node interop across the schema v4 flag day. merobox cannot
    test that by construction — every node is the same build against fresh
    state.

User-visible failure mode this guards against: "I revoked my stolen laptop and it kept reading our messages."
comment: Migrated from this file's v1 workflow by `merobox cloud port`.
Each of the original scenario's nodes is an account here; see merobox/cloud_v2/port.py for the mapping.
account_pair output credential (v1 device key) x1: checks what the dropped steps did
account_revoke output (v1 key rotation) x1: checks what the dropped steps did
json_assert statement on a dropped step's output x2: checks what the dropped steps did
login (unknown) x3: checks what the dropped steps did
wait_for_sync x7: replication is synchronous: a read sees every committed write
Migration note: v1's revoked device still held a local replica: it wrote locally
(allow_failure) and read the group as it was before the key rotation. Here a device
is a passkey and removing it ends its sessions, so each of its later calls, reads
included, is refused UNAUTHENTICATED; node-1's reads still check that none of them

steps.name: Install application on node-1
Node-1 creates namespace
Invite node-2 to the namespace
Node-2 joins the namespace
Node-1 creates the context
Node-2 enrolls a device for a fresh account
Node-2 writes from its first device
Node-1 reads the first device's write
The first device's write converged
Pair node-3 onto Alice's account
The pairing delivered a scope key and minted a credential
What node-3 speaks as, now that it is paired
Node-3 (paired device) writes
Node-1 reads the paired device's write
Both devices' writes converged
The two devices authored as one account but distinct replicas
What the phone speaks for
One account, two distinct devices
The account holder revokes node-3's device
The revoked device can no longer write
The surviving device still writes
Node-1 sees the survivor's write and not the revoked device's
Revocation cut out one device and only that device
Node-1 still sees the pre-revocation value for the revoked device's key
The revoked device's post-revocation write never landed
Give the recovery loop several rounds to try
The revoked device reads nothing, its session is gone
The revoked device still cannot write after the recovery window
Re-pair node-3 onto Alice's account
What node-3 speaks as after the re-pair
The re-pair minted a fresh device under the same account
